events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

what_happened_next.text:
Bonds led the seven choices. Cisco ended near 23 cents per starting dollar, while Microsoft and Amazon each ended around 51 cents. The U.S. share basket also fell, but much less than those three individual stocks. A useful technology or promising business could still disappoint investors who paid a high starting price.

Company reports show different kinds of pressure and progress. Cisco reported a $2.2 billion inventory charge in 2001 as sales weakened. Microsoft’s Windows XP system sold more than 67 million licenses by 2002. Amazon reported $6.92 billion in 2004 sales and $588 million in net income, including a large tax-accounting benefit. Those business facts help explain what was happening inside each company, but do not fully explain its share-price path.

The period included the September 11 attacks, euro notes and coins, and the loss of the Columbia shuttle. These events belong to the history of the five years, but do not explain the exact return of a software company, retailer or networking-equipment maker. A broad U.S. basket lost value too, but spread the risk across many businesses, reducing the loss here without preventing it.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Investors saw online books, internet broadcasting and networking equipment as signs of a changing economy. Taiwan’s election and scientific discoveries competed for attention.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The price paid and the full five-year path mattered. Spreading money across many companies reduced dependence on these three badly hit shares.
reflection.what_faded_away: The number of people downloading a story did not reveal a software or networking company’s future return. Exciting new habits were not automatic stock-market gains.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew the size of the losses ahead. The internet’s importance did not make every share price reasonable or every company a winner.

hot:2000-03:cisco.text: On May 8, 2001, Cisco reported quarterly sales of $4.73 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. It recorded a $2.2 billion charge for excess inventory and a $2.69 billion net loss as orders for networking equipment slowed sharply.

hot:2000-03:microsoft.text: By October 2002, Microsoft said more than 67 million Windows XP licenses had sold since its October 2001 launch. But $1 invested in Microsoft in March 2000 ended near 52 cents five years later, showing that strong software sales did not prevent a falling share value.

hot:2000-03:amazon.text: Amazon reported 2004 sales of $6.92 billion, up 31%, and net income of $588 million. It said a one-time $244 million tax-accounting benefit boosted reported profit, so regular business earnings were lower than the headline suggested. The results still showed a much larger retailer with positive earnings.
